summary:
Putumayo department stands under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Partner recognition is settled in the visitor's favour. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to premises and to custody are governed by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Against that framework sits lethal violence, and no source in this inventory reports a trans-specific killing, threat or police response inside Putumayo itself. The national pattern is the operative context: 13 trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024, and 41 were killed in 2023. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025.

On 5 April 2025 a video went viral showing Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia and flailing in a creek before she drowned; international reporting states she died of a second cardiac arrest at three the following afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no one was arrested. President Gustavo Petro asked authorities to investigate urgently, and solidarity events were held in several cities to denounce transphobia. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." International reporting also recalls earlier fatal attacks: gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and trans people killed in their homes or in a hairdresser.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed groups. Caqueta department, which borders Putumayo, is the clearest documented case: three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed, and she fled at night after hiding for a week. "Social cleansing" flyers appeared on Caqueta streets and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Discrimination limits trans women in the country mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
The distance between statute and street is the central pattern for a visitor. Colombia's identification, marriage and premises rules are settled and visitor-favourable, yet international press documents killings that continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Caqueta offers the nearest comparison for Putumayo, both because it shares a border and because it shows the mechanism: armed-group flyer campaigns, direct death threats against named trans women, and displacement rather than arrest. International reporting found discrimination confining trans women to hairdressing or sex work, which shapes where a trans visitor is likely to be approached, watched or exposed.

Investigations into high-profile anti-trans killings have produced no arrests in at least one documented case, even where police interrogated local residents and the head of state ordered an urgent inquiry. Institutional reform and investigative follow-through are not the same thing.

outOfScopeNotes:
None of the sources in this inventory reports a trans-specific killing, threat, arrest or police response located in Putumayo. The violence findings are national figures or cases from Antioquia, Caqueta and Guajira; treating any of them as a Putumayo event would be unsupported.

Whether the Ministry of Interior decree, the premises judgments and the notary procedure are applied as written by officials in Putumayo is unresolved. No source here records implementation, refusal or delay at department level.

Police handling of anti-trans complaints in Putumayo is not sourced. The one documented investigation of a high-profile 2025 killing recorded no arrests, but that case arose in another department.

The status of the comprehensive trans bill referred to in earlier drafting of this record is not established by the sources supplied for this pass and should be verified against current legislative records before publication.

Entry screening and visa practice for trans travellers at Colombian border and airport points are not covered by this inventory; the partner-recognition and visa-equivalence claims concern spouses of Colombian residents, not general admission decisions.
